title: Breaking and Entering with Cate Le Bon
summary: Cate Le Bon discusses her new record, Reward.
transcript:
Cate Le Bon spoke by phone with Lauren Taylor and Simon Winkler for an interview broadcast on Breaking and Entering on 7 November 2019, discussing her fifth album, Reward, and the furniture-making course she undertook while writing it. The conversation began with ‘Miami’ and the associations created by locating a song in a particular place. Edited for length and clarity.

Cate: There’s always a danger in it, where you’re anchoring something so specifically. There’s something to me being from a small village in West Wales and singing about Miami off the bat. It’s almost comical because I don’t think you could get anywhere more opposite to where I grew up than Miami. There’s an immediate disparity, and I like that kind of absurdity. The song is not about Miami at all. It just happened to be the place where I was when a real palpable change happened in my life. I just remember thinking, Christ, it’s so strange that this is happening, and I’m in Miami.

Lauren: Reward was written alongside an intensive 12-month furniture course at Waters & Acland in Staveley. You’ve spoken about committing to furniture to re-evaluate your relationship with music and figure out what you wanted from it. What did you learn about that relationship through the process?

Cate: The most important thing was committing myself to something else so wholeheartedly. I’d reached a point where I’d been touring for so long and making music for so long, but I wasn’t sure if I was doing it out of habit or whether I still possessed a real joy and love for it. It was quite a relief to find out during that year that it was still something I very much loved doing. I just needed to address the terms on which I did it and how I executed certain things. It was an important time to take to restructure certain things.

Simon: You said something interesting about studying at Waters & Acland: we’re always waiting for someone to give us permission, but you have to give yourself that pass to do something. How hard was it to make the decision to step off the train and check your priorities?

Cate: I’d reached a point where I kept saying I was just going to give music up, not in any kind of ‘woe is me’ way. If you’re not getting the joy and the reward from it anymore, then there’s little point in doing it. Once that exit door has been painted in your mind, you can explore less severe ways of readdressing your relationship instead of ending it. I suppose it was like couples counselling of sorts, to put your attention on something else. Once the onus was taken off music, it’s like trying to catch a horse in a field. Sometimes once you stop looking at the horse, that’s when it comes to you. It was a lovely way to rediscover that joy I once had for it. It’s nice to know it’s still there, especially when you dedicate so much time to something. Like any job, there are sacrifices you make, and you want to know that it’s worth it, I suppose.

Simon: It takes courage to commit to that process of learning, relocating and evaluating that relationship.

Cate: You make a series of decisions, and I don’t think I’d fully comprehended how it was going to change the whole architecture of my life until I was on my own in a cottage in the Lake District, going to school every day. It felt pretty surreal for a while and took some getting used to. Putting yourself in a position where you feel a little uncomfortable is something I’ve always tried to do. I always try to put myself in a bit of a vacuum so that you’re never pulled in different ways from some invented expectation you think people have of you, or an invented audience you’re imagining. It’s scary, but nice to know that the buck stops with you and you have to make decisions you can stand by. That’s something I’ve always tried to do.

Lauren: Precision comes up in conversations about Reward. It’s key to making furniture: if things aren’t lined up at every stage, the end product becomes a misaligned mess. Is there more room to manoeuvre when you’re putting together a song?

Cate: When you make a piece of furniture, there’s a strict order of process. When you’re making music, anything goes, really. You can always come back to a point and readdress something later down the line. But strangely, the songs I’d written for Reward had been with me during that year, and they’d become so solid in their form that there wasn’t much manipulating of the songs or the form when we got into the studio. Much like when you’re working with a piece of wood, you’re beholden to your material. It went that way in the studio, and it’s never happened to me before when I was making a record, where you’re so anchored to what the song demands. I ended up having to craft and really sit down and write particular parts of stuff and slot things together in a way I haven’t done on previous records. The two processes overlapped at certain points, for sure. At times they couldn’t be further apart from one another.

Simon: Another element you’ve talked about that’s common to both furniture making and songwriting is patience. You’ve spent more time with these songs than perhaps previously. What did being patient give you or teach you about songwriting?

Cate: My records have always employed continuity, and it’s always been something I felt excited by. The song I was working with had a spontaneous element to the writing. I think you always have to serve the songs. Thankfully, with this group of songs, I’d learnt to be patient during the process of learning furniture building. At times while making the record, it was more that nobody really knew what to do. You’ve got to learn to step away and let it come to you, as opposed to potching with something until you have to start again. Sometimes in school I’d spend two weeks making a jig to make one cut, but that cut had to be so precise. Otherwise you’d have to go back to getting a piece of wood from a tree and machining it to the right dimension. You’d have to revert right back to the beginning of the process. I guess it’s about knowing when to put the brakes on, take your hands away from something and really think about your next move and the knock-on effect of it. I don’t think I’d ever learnt patience before. It was more: plug your guitar in, get a sound you really love, then do something spontaneous. That just didn’t fly with this record at all. It was a lot of sitting down and spending time crafting parts that interweaved with the song and the vocal melodies. It was quite the learning curve, frustrating at times, but really enjoyable when something clicked and you got somewhere with it.

Lauren: You made a chair that represents something of the essence of Reward when you were a woodworker in residence. How do you translate something like Reward into an item of furniture?

Simon: Can you also describe the finished piece for those who haven’t seen it?

Cate: The finished piece is quite a brutal chair. After the fact, I was thinking maybe it was inspired more by my relationship with the album than the album itself, if that makes sense. It’s difficult to put into words, which is why I put it into a chair, maybe.
